newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh talks with tribal rebels inconclusive.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh talks with tribal rebels inconclusive.

text.p: Latest talks between the government and tribal rebels to end a 23-year insurgency in southeastern Bangladesh ended in Dhaka on Saturday without agreement.
But negotiators said they would meet again soon.

"We are still in the process of working out the draft of a (peace) deal. We will meet soon," Abul Hasnat Abdullah, chief government negotiator, told reporters before the rebel team left Dhaka on Saturday. The two sides have met five times so far this year.

The rebel team, led by Jyotirindra Budhipriya Larma, head of the Parbattya Chattagram Jana Sanghati Samity (PCJSS), the political wing of the tribal Shanti Bahini guerrillas, was due to fly by military helicopter to Dudukchhari, a tribal hamlet, bordering the northeastern Indian state of Tripura.
Abdullah, chief parliamentary whip of the ruling Awami League, said the schedule of the next meeting would be set through discussions between the two sides.

Talks had resumed on Monday as part of the government's efforts to end the insurgency in the 5,500 sq-mile (14,200 sq-km) Chittagong Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma, where the Shanti Bahini demanded political autonomy.
It also asked for the expulsion of some 500,000 Bengali-speaking settlers from the region, which the rebels consider a tribal homeland.

Government officials said after the previous meeting in May that broad outlines of a treaty had already been agreed but the PCJSS was facing opposition from a group of Shanti Bahini hardliners and several supporting groups, including the Hill Students Council.

This led to widespread speculation of a breakthrough in the latest talks, but sources involved in the meeting said on Saturday that fresh disputes over repatriation and rehabilitation of tribal refugees from Tripura had complicated the issue.
They said the rebel leaders expressed displeasure at the rehabilitation process of the tribal refugees who returned home recently.
"They (rebels) want the repatriated refugees to be immediately given formal ownership of land," said one official, who declined to be identified,
"Some hardliners even asked that the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) be involved in the repatriation and rehabilitation process," he said.
The insurgency, in which over 8,500 rebels, soldiers and civilians have been killed, forced some 50,000 tribespeople to flee into Tripura over the past decade.
Nearly 7,000 refugees returned home in March and April following an agreement between Dhaka and New Delhi, but officials say it remains uncertain when the next phase of repatriation will start.
